scenario.title: Support backlog
scenario.initial_request: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds

M-IBAN-FAILURE-SHARE.name: Share of sampled refund failure records with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT

M-TICKET-RESPONSE-TIME.name: Median ticket response time versus SLA

M-REFUND-BACKLOG-RESOLUTION-RA.name: Rate of FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds resolved or corrected
M-REFUND-BACKLOG-RESOLUTION-RA.denominator: total refunds currently with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT

F-01.statement: payment-db refund_failures query returned 5 records, all with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT.

F-02.statement: ticket-db response_times query (900 tickets) shows a median response time of 2.0 hours against a 24-hour SLA.

CL-01.statement: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds

CL-02.statement: Customers wait forever; a chatbot would answer instantly.

H-NO-AUTOMATED-CHANNEL.statement: Customers experience long waits for refund answers because there is no self-service/chatbot channel to answer status questions; building a chatbot would resolve the backlog.

H-SLOW-REFUND-PROCESSING.statement: The underlying refund process (payment execution/approval) is itself slow, so customers wait regardless of how they ask; a chatbot would surface delays faster but not reduce them.

H-SUPPORT-CAPACITY-SHORTAGE.statement: Support staff cannot keep up with refund-related ticket volume (a capacity/staffing problem), producing the backlog described in the scenario title, independent of channel type.

H-STATUS-VISIBILITY-GAP.statement: Customers wait because they lack proactive visibility into refund status (not because they need a conversational chatbot); a simpler status-lookup feature would resolve the complaint equally well.

H-IBAN-FORMAT-FAILURE.statement: Refunds are stuck/unresolved because they fail outright with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT, creating a backlog that no chatbot, status feature, or added staffing can clear without fixing the underlying IBAN data defect.

interpretation_history.interpretation: All 5 sampled refund_failures records in payment-db have status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT, showing refund payments are stalling due to a payment-data defect rather than merely being slow or hard to track. This reveals a technical processing failure mode as a backlog driver, independent of the customer communication channel assumed by the initial chatbot request.

Ticket-db shows support agents respond to tickets quickly (median 2.0 hours) well inside the 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets, indicating the support team is not slow or overwhelmed in answering customer tickets; this weakens channel/capacity-based explanations for the 'waiting' complaint and leaves the already-observed payment IBAN-format failures (E-01) as the more plausible backlog driver.

E-03.content: Customers wait forever; a chatbot would answer instantly.

interpretation_history.interpretation: SH-SUP's interview statement reiterates the initial request framing (CL-01) that waiting is a channel/speed problem solvable by a chatbot; it adds no new technical evidence and reflects the stakeholder's documented bias toward framing issues as response speed. It does not address or explain the IBAN-format payment failures (E-01) already established as a backlog driver.

U-BACKLOG-POPULATION-SIZE.question: What is the full size of the FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT backlog across all refunds, beyond the 5-record sample (payment-db completeness is UNKNOWN)?
U-BACKLOG-POPULATION-SIZE.decision_impact: Determines how large the remediation effort needs to be and whether the IBAN defect is the dominant backlog driver or one of several.
U-BACKLOG-POPULATION-SIZE.resolution_path: Query payment-db for the full count/trend of refund_failures by status across the entire dataset, not just the 5-record sample.
U-BACKLOG-POPULATION-SIZE.safe_placeholder: Treat the 100% FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT rate in the sample as indicative only; do not size remediation investment until the full backlog count is confirmed.

U-IBAN-DEFECT-ROOT-CAUSE.question: What upstream source produces the invalid IBAN data (customer input, migration, third-party integration)?
U-IBAN-DEFECT-ROOT-CAUSE.decision_impact: Determines whether the fix is a data-validation change at intake, a backend data-correction job, or a customer re-entry flow.
U-IBAN-DEFECT-ROOT-CAUSE.resolution_path: Inspect payment-db schema/source and trace a sample of FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records back to their origin.
U-IBAN-DEFECT-ROOT-CAUSE.safe_placeholder: Do not design an automated correction mechanism until the root cause is identified; handle known failing cases manually in the interim.

U-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE.question: Do the support tickets about refund waits correspond specifically to the FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds, or are they a broader population?
U-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE.decision_impact: Confirms whether fixing the IBAN defect will actually reduce the refund-related ticket volume driving the complaint.
U-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE.resolution_path: Join ticket-db records with payment-db refund_failures on refund id to measure overlap.
U-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE.safe_placeholder: Assume plausible but unconfirmed correlation; do not claim ticket-volume reduction as a guaranteed outcome of the IBAN fix.

U-TICKET-SCOPE-SPECIFICITY.question: Does the 900-ticket sample behind E-02's 2.0h median response time include refund-status tickets specifically, or all support tickets generally?
U-TICKET-SCOPE-SPECIFICITY.decision_impact: If the fast response finding is not refund-ticket-specific, confidence in rejecting channel/capacity-based explanations for refund tickets is weaker.
U-TICKET-SCOPE-SPECIFICITY.resolution_path: Filter ticket-db response_times by refund-related ticket category/tag if such a filter exists.
U-TICKET-SCOPE-SPECIFICITY.safe_placeholder: Treat the SLA-compliance finding as indicative of overall support responsiveness, not confirmed refund-ticket-specific responsiveness, pending filtering.

A-SAMPLE-REPRESENTATIVE.statement: The 5 sampled refund_failures records are representative of the broader refund-failure population, not an unrepresentative slice.

A-IBAN-FAILURE-BLOCKS-COMPLETI.statement: A FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT status means the refund payment cannot complete and stays unresolved, rather than being a transient/auto-retried state.

SC-BACKLOG-ELIMINATED.statement: All refunds currently stuck with FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT are resolved or corrected.
SC-BACKLOG-ELIMINATED.validation_method: Re-query payment-db refund_failures and confirm zero remaining FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records.

SC-SLA-MAINTAINED.statement: Ticket response time remains within the existing SLA while the refund issue is addressed.
SC-SLA-MAINTAINED.validation_method: Re-query ticket-db response_times and confirm median_hours <= sla_hours.

SC-BACKLOG-SIZED.statement: The full population size of FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds beyond the 5-record sample is quantified.
SC-BACKLOG-SIZED.validation_method: Query payment-db for the complete count of refund_failures by status across the entire dataset.

problem_definition.requested_solution: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds.
symptoms: Customers report waiting a long time for answers about refund status.
All 5 sampled payment-db refund_failures records show status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01).
Support ticket median response time is 2.0h against a 24h SLA across 900 tickets (E-02), i.e. support is not slow.
problem_definition.root_problem: Refunds in the refund process (P-REF) remain unresolved and create a customer-facing backlog because they fail during payment execution with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01), not because support lacks a fast-response channel, since ticket response times are well within SLA (E-02).

decision_log.rationale: causal chain: Refund payment execution requires a validly formatted IBAN on the payout record. → Some refund payments carry invalid IBAN data, causing payment-db to mark them with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01: 5/5 sampled refund_failures records). → A refund in FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT status does not complete payment, leaving the refund unresolved and the customer's refund request stuck. → Customers with stuck refunds perceive this as 'waiting forever' for an answer and raise support tickets. → Support agents respond to those tickets quickly (median 2.0h vs 24h SLA, E-02), so the perceived wait is driven by the unresolved payment itself, not by slow ticket handling or lack of a chatbot channel.; rejected framings: [('H-NO-AUTOMATED-CHANNEL', 'Contradicted by E-01 and E-02: refunds fail outright with a technical status (FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT) and support already responds quickly, so a chatbot channel would not clear the backlog.'), ('H-SLOW-REFUND-PROCESSING', 'Contradicted by E-01: the records show a hard failure status (FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT), not generic processing slowness, so faster surfacing of delays would not help.'), ('H-STATUS-VISIBILITY-GAP', 'Contradicted by E-01: the issue is that refunds fail to complete, not that customers merely lack visibility into an otherwise progressing refund.'), ('H-SUPPORT-CAPACITY-SHORTAGE', 'Contradicted by E-02: median response time (2.0h) is well within the 24h SLA, showing no capacity/staffing shortfall.')]
[CONDITIONAL] critical unknown U-BACKLOG-POPULATION-SIZE deferred to VOB-U-BACKLOG-POPULATION-SIZE; [CONDITIONAL] critical unknown U-IBAN-DEFECT-ROOT-CAUSE deferred to VOB-U-IBAN-DEFECT-ROOT-CAUSE

causal_chain: Refund payment execution requires a validly formatted IBAN on the payout record.
Some refund payments carry invalid IBAN data, causing payment-db to mark them with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01: 5/5 sampled refund_failures records).
A refund in FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT status does not complete payment, leaving the refund unresolved and the customer's refund request stuck.
Customers with stuck refunds perceive this as 'waiting forever' for an answer and raise support tickets.

Support agents respond to those tickets quickly (median 2.0h vs 24h SLA, E-02), so the perceived wait is driven by the unresolved payment itself, not by slow ticket handling or lack of a chatbot channel.

key_points: The initial request from stakeholder SH-SUP was 'Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds' (CL-01, CL-02), framing the problem as a missing automated communication channel.

Evidence E-01 (5 sampled payment-db refund_failures records, all status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT) and E-02 (ticket-db: median 2.0h response time vs 24h SLA across 900 tickets) were gathered to test that framing.

E-02 shows support response times are well within SLA, so the hypothesis that slow support/no chatbot causes the wait (H-NO-AUTOMATED-CHANNEL) was REJECTED, along with H-SLOW-REFUND-PROCESSING, H-STATUS-VISIBILITY-GAP and H-SUPPORT-CAPACITY-SHORTAGE.

The hypothesis H-IBAN-FORMAT-FAILURE (refunds are stuck because they fail with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT, a payment-data defect, not a communication gap) is SUPPORTED by E-01 and E-02 and was marked CRITICAL decision impact; it defines the root problem in PD-1.

The DEFINE gate for PD-1 returned CONDITIONAL_PASS, deferring two HIGH-criticality unknowns (U-BACKLOG-POPULATION-SIZE, U-IBAN-DEFECT-ROOT-CAUSE) to open verification obligations VOB-U-BACKLOG-POPULATION-SIZE and VOB-U-IBAN-DEFECT-ROOT-CAUSE.
The release decision is RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION; the actual release_scope in SD-1 is limited to correlate_tickets_with_failed_refunds:DA-TCK, which matches the minimum_useful_scope.

The two actions that would size the backlog and find its root cause (quantify_iban_failure_backlog, investigate_iban_defect_root_cause) are excluded from this release because their blocking VOBs (VOB-U-BACKLOG-POPULATION-SIZE, VOB-U-IBAN-DEFECT-ROOT-CAUSE) remain OPEN and lie outside the release scope.

A medium-impact open question, VOB-R-3, intersects the released scope: whether tickets matched by correlate_tickets_with_failed_refunds specifically concern FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds or a broader population (U-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE, U-TICKET-SCOPE-SPECIFICITY).
limitations_explained: The DEFINE gate for this problem only reached CONDITIONAL_PASS, not a full pass; the deferred items are tracked as open verification obligations rather than resolved.
VOB-U-BACKLOG-POPULATION-SIZE (how many refunds in total have FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT, beyond the 5-record sample E-01) is still OPEN and its scope (quantify_iban_failure_backlog) is outside this release.
VOB-U-IBAN-DEFECT-ROOT-CAUSE (what upstream source produces the invalid IBAN data) is still OPEN and its scope (investigate_iban_defect_root_cause) is outside this release.
VOB-R-3 is non-critical but overlaps the released scope: it is not yet confirmed whether the correlated tickets specifically concern FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds or a broader refund/ticket population.

The current conclusion that FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT is the cause rests on only 5 sampled payment-db records (E-01); the completeness of payment-db and ticket-db (DA-PAY, DA-TCK) is UNKNOWN, so the finding covers only currently available records, not necessarily the whole population.

Two remedies that would actually remove the root cause - adding IBAN format validation upstream (SR-UPSTREAM-IBAN-INPUT-VALIDATI) and a payments-team backfill/correction process (SR-IBAN-BACKLOG-CORRECTION-PROC) - were identified but not implemented, because no write/deploy tool exists in this harness to carry them out.
As a result, success criterion SC-BACKLOG-ELIMINATED (all FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds resolved) cannot be met by this release; only the ticket-correlation work item was completed and released.
proposal.summary: The stakeholder SH-SUP initially asked for a chatbot so customers stop waiting for refund answers (CL-01, CL-02), framing the issue as a missing communication channel. Investigation evidence showed support ticket response times are fast and within SLA (E-02: 2.0h median vs 24h SLA, 900 tickets), while a sample of payment-db refund records all showed status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01). This supported the hypothesis H-IBAN-FORMAT-FAILURE that refunds are actually stuck due to an IBAN data defect in payment processing, not a lack of chatbot/communication capacity; competing hypotheses about channel, process speed, visibility, and staffing capacity were all rejected. The problem definition (PD-1) passed its DEFINE gate only as CONDITIONAL_PASS, deferring two high-criticality unknowns about backlog size and root cause to open verification obligations. The release decision is RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION: only the ticket-to-refund correlation action was released, while the backlog-sizing and root-cause-investigation actions were excluded because their blocking verification obligations remain open and outside release scope. Known limitations include small/unverified sample completeness, an open question about whether correlated tickets specifically concern IBAN-failed refunds, and the fact that no tool exists to implement the two remedies that would actually fix the underlying IBAN defect, so full backlog elimination is not achievable within this harness.
